segments: The Chronography of Barhebraeus.
to Trajan,
that no other fault could be found in the Christians,
except that they were not willing to sacrifice to idols;
and that they hated adultery, and murder, and every shameful deed.
And when Caesar learned these things,
he commanded that they should not be sought out (pursued).
Except that when any one of them was found,
he should be judged until he sacrificed.
And in his tenth year, Galen the physician was born.
And at the end of his reign, the Jews who were in Cyprus uprooted Salamis {OCR: Salōmōnī, to Salamina?}, the city,
and slaughtered {OCR: for ܩܛܠܘ} the Greeks who were in it.
And also the Jews who were in Libya stirred up strife against the Greeks who were there.
And likewise those in Cyrene, and the Thebaid, and Alexandria, and Mesopotamia; and the Jews who were in Egypt also rebelled,
and set up over themselves a king whose name was Lukuas {OCR: Lūmpīs?}.
And he led them and came to Judea.
Then the Jews prevailed (were defeated? {or: the Greeks}) in every place.
And Basilides, the head of the Gnostic heresy—that is, the serpent-worshippers—became known.
After Trajan, Hadrian {OCR: Ṭ...rīnos for Hadrīyānōs} Caesar [reigned] twenty-one years.
When he became king,
he made a cancellation of debts,
and remitted many tributes to many [people],
burning the promissory notes of the debts of the cities.
And in his fourth year, the kingdom was abolished from Edessa,
and governors administered affairs there as in every [other] place.
And in his fifth year,
the river Cephisus {OCR: Pīsōs, for Qēpīsōs?} flooded Eleusis {OCR: Elūsīnā}.
And Hadrian built a bridge over it,
and built a portico {OCR?} in Athens.
And in his time there were:
Claudius Ptolemy the astronomer, who made the book of the Megiste, and called it the Syntaxis;
and Galen the physician was learning and teaching;
and Secundus the silent philosopher became known,
in that, when Hadrian marveled [at him],
he desired to break his silence,
but he was resolute even unto death.
And a certain Jew whose name was Bar Kokhba rebelled in Judea,
and took captive and killed those who would not submit to him.
The king, however, sent an army and devastated the Jews,
and completely uprooted Jerusalem.
And they built a city there,
and called it Aelia Capitolina {OCR: Hēlyōs Adryānōs},
and settled foreign nations in it.
